articles.title: 'A música não está separada da política', diz duo espanhol Iseo & Dodosound, que se apresenta nesta sexta em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Com mistura de reggae, dub e música eletrônica, artistas falam sobre questões sociais nas canções e defendem intercâmbio musical entre Brasil, Espanha e América Latina. Banda se apresenta nesta sexta-feira (8) no Cine Joia, no Centro.
articles.summary: Com mistura de reggae, dub e música eletrônica, artistas falam sobre questões sociais nas canções e defendem intercâmbio musical entre Brasil, Espanha e América Latina. Banda se apresenta nesta sexta-feira (8) no Cine Joia, no Centro.
articles.body:
Duo espanhol Iseo & Dodosound. — Foto: Divulgação

A mistura de reggae, dub, música eletrônica e trip hop é a marca do duo espanhol Iseo & Dodosound, que há 12 anos constrói uma sonoridade influenciada pela cultura dos sound systems jamaicanos. Mas, para os artistas, a música vai além dos ritmos. Ela também é uma forma de expressar preocupações sociais e políticas.

“Não somos um grupo político, mas sempre estamos fazendo política”, afirma Alberto García Iriarte, conhecido como Dodosound, ao lado da cantora Leire Villanueva, a "Iseo", em entrevista ao g1 , realizada na quarta-feira (7), por chamada de vídeo. "A música não está separada da política."

O duo terminava de fechar as malas para vir ao Brasil. A dupla se apresenta nesta sexta-feira (9), no Cine Joia, na região central de São Paulo . O show integra a programação do "Mucho! Ciudad Sonora" e marca a terceira passagem do grupo pelo Brasil.

Segundo Dodosound, as questões que afetam a sociedade também atravessam o trabalho dos artistas. Isso aparece nas letras, nos shows e nas mensagens que a dupla procura transmitir ao público.

“Temos de prestar atenção a essas problemáticas, dedicar-lhes alguns versos, mostrar nosso descontentamento, mostrar nossa solidariedade também, fazer uma espécie de refúgio diante deste fascismo que nos atropela agora”, diz o músico.

Para Leire, essa relação é inseparável da própria experiência de viver em sociedade. A cantora afirma que sentimentos como raiva, frustração e solidariedade diante de situações injustas acabam aparecendo nas composições.

“Todos vivemos em sociedade e, no nosso caso, como artistas, isso aparece na nossa arte”, afirma.

A relação com o público brasileiro é uma das razões pelas quais a dupla diz ter expectativa para o retorno ao país. A primeira passagem pela América Latina aconteceu em 2018. Depois de voltar ao Brasil em 2025, os músicos se apresentam novamente em São Paulo.

Para Leire, a música tem a capacidade de aproximar pessoas de diferentes países mesmo quando elas não compreendem a língua das canções. Ela vê um movimento crescente de intercâmbio entre artistas latino-americanos e espanhóis, embora a distância e os custos de viagens ainda dificultem a circulação de grupos independentes.

A cantora avalia que o público tem ampliado o interesse por músicas em idiomas diferentes do inglês, movimento que pode favorecer a aproximação entre cenas musicais. Para ela, essa troca entre América Latina e Espanha já está em curso, mas precisa de tempo para se fortalecer.

"A música é uma forma de criar pontes. Afinal, todos nós ouvimos músicas cujas letras nem sempre entendemos, seja pela língua ou por qualquer outro motivo", diz.

Dodosound lembra que a música brasileira já tem uma história de circulação na Espanha. Ele cita artistas como Caetano Veloso e Carlinhos Brown entre os nomes que chegaram ao público espanhol e destaca a presença de canções brasileiras nas rádios do país.

Leire, por sua vez, aponta a bossa nova e nomes como Gilberto Gil e Caetano Veloso entre suas principais referências brasileiras.

Apesar dessa conexão cultural, Dodosound afirma que a distância geográfica continua sendo um obstáculo para a troca entre músicos dos dois países.

A apresentação em São Paulo acontece durante a turnê de “Volando”, quinto álbum de estúdio do duo, lançado em 2026. O disco é o segundo trabalho inteiramente cantado em castelhano, depois de “En la Tormenta”, de 2024.

Na Espanha, o castelhano, ou espanhol, é a língua oficial do Estado e é falado em diversos países da América Latina, como México, Argentina, Colômbia, Chile e Peru. O país também tem outras línguas oficiais em determinadas regiões, como o catalão, o galego e o basco. Embora compartilhem o espanhol, os países latino-americanos desenvolveram sotaques, expressões e particularidades próprias, influenciadas por suas histórias e culturas.

Segundo Dodosound, a decisão de compor no idioma foi acontecendo naturalmente. No início da carreira, a dupla escrevia principalmente em inglês, língua presente em boa parte da música que os influenciava. Com o tempo, o castelhano passou a ganhar espaço até se tornar a língua de um álbum inteiro.

Para o músico, cantar no próprio idioma permite explorar outras possibilidades de expressão e composição.

Ele também diz que a escolha foi uma maneira de se aproximar do público que acompanhava a dupla e esperava ouvir um disco em espanhol. A experiência foi bem recebida, e a dupla decidiu manter o idioma em “Volando”, sem descartar composições futuras em inglês ou outras línguas.

Apesar da mudança no idioma e da experiência acumulada ao longo de cinco álbuns, Leire afirma que o duo não procura transformar radicalmente sua sonoridade a cada lançamento.

A cantora compara a evolução musical do grupo ao curso de um rio: o caminho muda, ganha velocidade ou faz curvas, mas preserva sua essência. A liberdade para experimentar, segundo ela, continua sendo um dos princípios do projeto.

articles.title: Bolsa de sangue raro cruza o país na cabine de avião comercial para chegar a paciente transplantado  | G1
articles.standfirst: Internado em Juiz de Fora (MG) após um transplante de rim, paciente tem anticorpo contra um marcador presente no sangue da maioria dos brasileiros, e só seis doadores cadastrados podem atendê-lo. A bolsa colhida no Ceará viajou com o piloto, nos primeiros casos de um novo acordo do Ministério da Saúde com as companhias aéreas.
articles.summary: Internado em Juiz de Fora (MG) após um transplante de rim, paciente tem anticorpo contra um marcador presente no sangue da maioria dos brasileiros, e só seis doadores cadastrados podem atendê-lo. A bolsa colhida no Ceará viajou com o piloto, nos primeiros casos de um novo acordo do Ministério da Saúde com as companhias aéreas.
articles.body:
Um paciente internado em Juiz de Fora (MG) precisava de um tipo de sangue que, no cadastro nacional, somente seis pessoas no Brasil podem oferecer . Uma delas mora no Ceará. Na quinta-feira (8), ela chegou cedo ao hemocentro do estado para doar, e a bolsa de sangue deixou o aeroporto às 18h dentro da cabine de um avião comercial, aos cuidados do piloto.

É um tipo de transporte que o Ministério da Saúde está formalizando com as companhias aéreas e que, até agora, só valia para órgãos. A chegada a Confins, na Região Metropolitana de Belo Horizonte, está prevista para as 5h desta sexta-feira (9). De lá, o sangue segue de carro até o hospital, onde será transfundido ainda pela manhã.

Quem espera a bolsa é um paciente que passou por transplante de rim , está estável e precisa de sangue porque a hemoglobina está baixa. O problema apareceu quando a equipe médica testou o sangue dele para a transfusão e encontrou um anticorpo que reagia contra as células vermelhas, as hemácias, usadas nos exames.

Novos testes mostraram a causa: o organismo do paciente produz anticorpos contra o Jsb , um marcador presente na superfície dessas células. Quase todo mundo tem o Jsb, e quem não tem não pode receber sangue que o carregue.

Um tipo sanguíneo que vai além de A, B, AB e O

A maioria das pessoas conhece o tipo sanguíneo pela carteirinha: A, B, AB ou O, positivo ou negativo. Mas esse é só o começo. A superfície das células vermelhas do sangue, as hemácias, tem centenas de outras “etiquetas” que o laboratório não costuma checar. É o que explica a hematologista Fernanda de Oliveira Santos, integrante da Associação Brasileira de Hematologia, Hemoterapia e Terapia Celular e da Sociedade Brasileira de Trombose e Hemostasia.

Uma dessas etiquetas se chama Jsb, e quase todo mundo a tem. O paciente de Juiz de Fora não tem, e seu organismo produz anticorpos que reagem contra ela. Por isso, as defesas dele atacam o sangue de quase todos os doadores, e ele só pode receber o de quem também não tem a etiqueta, o que é muito raro . Além disso, o sangue precisa ser do tipo O, o mesmo dele.

A incompatibilidade só aparece porque os hospitais fazem um teste de segurança em todas as transfusões. Antes de liberar qualquer bolsa, o laboratório mistura uma gota do sangue do paciente com uma amostra do sangue do doador. Se as células se juntam em grumos, o que os médicos chamam de aglutinação , a bolsa não serve. Foi o que aconteceu com ele.

O teste existe para impedir que o organismo destrua o sangue recebido , um processo que provoca inflamação e que, segundo a hematologista, pode ser grave mesmo quando demora a aparecer.

Quando um hospital não encontra sangue compatível, a busca começa em bancos de sangue parceiros e, se nenhum tiver a bolsa, chega ao cadastro nacional de doadores raros , que reúne 2.032 pessoas.

Como poucos laboratórios conseguem identificar esse tipo de anticorpo, as amostras costumam seguir para serviços mais complexos, que confirmam a raridade.

Os nomes entram na lista a partir de doações comuns: quando o laboratório percebe que o sangue de alguém é incomum –o chamado ‘sangue raro’--, convida a pessoa a se cadastrar.

No caso do paciente de Juiz de Fora, o pedido chegou ao Ministério da Saúde entre 16h e 17h de quarta-feira (7), e o cadastro indicou seis doadores no país inteiro.

O doador do Ceará foi avisado às 22h e confirmou que poderia ir . Não foi a distância que decidiu, e sim estar apto naquele dia: quem doou há pouco tempo precisa esperar, 60 dias no caso dos homens e 90 no das mulheres. Quem entra no cadastro sabe que o telefone pode tocar e é orientado a não doar com frequência, para continuar disponível quando alguém precisar.

O Hemocentro do Ceará, que tem mais doadores raros cadastrados do que qualquer outro serviço do país, repetiu os testes para confirmar que o sangue era mesmo igual ao que o paciente precisava e acelerou os exames que descartam doenças como HIV e hepatites B e C, que normalmente levam cerca de dois dias. A identidade do doador é mantida em sigilo.

Acordo pode oficializar inclusão de sangue raro

A bolsa de 450 mililitros seguiu em uma caixa térmica preparada para manter a temperatura de geladeira por até 24 horas , com material de resfriamento calculado para a duração da viagem. Ela viajou na cabine do piloto . A companhia aérea escolheu o voo mais rápido e autorizou o transporte, com documentação encaminhada pelo Sistema Nacional de Transplantes.

A mudança vem de um novo arranjo, negociado neste ano, entre o Ministério da Saúde, a Agência Nacional de Aviação Civil (Anac) e as companhias aéreas. O acordo de cooperação técnica que já previa o transporte de rim, fígado, coração e pulmão na cabine está sendo reformulado para incluir também as bolsas de sangue raro.

Segundo a coordenadora-geral de sangue e hemoderivados do ministério, Luciana Maria de Barros Carlos, a política do sangue passa a seguir o modelo que já funciona nos transplantes , e o caso de Juiz de Fora está entre os primeiros em que ela é aplicada.

Em entrevista ao g1 , ela afirma que as empresas já fazem o transporte, mesmo antes da assinatura do novo termo, sem cobrar do hospital nem do hemocentro.

Uma bolsa pode não bastar. Outros dois doadores do cadastro foram acionados para o caso de novas transfusões nesse paciente, e a equipe do ministério o acompanha junto com o hemocentro e o hospital até que ele saia da situação crítica, para não convocar ninguém à toa nem tarde demais.

Segundo Luciana, sem esse preparo prévio, encontrar o doador certo a tempo seria como procurar uma agulha em um palheiro.

O ministério trabalha agora em duas frentes para encurtar esse caminho . Uma é o congelamento de bolsas de sangue raro . Hoje, cada pedido exige localizar um doador, esperar que ele possa ir ao hemocentro e colher a bolsa. Com as bolsas congeladas, será possível guardá-las para quando surgir um paciente.

A Pasta já negocia com a vigilância sanitária as soluções necessárias para o procedimento, e a expectativa é que as primeiras bolsas possam ser congeladas a partir de janeiro, o que, segundo Luciana, deve dar mais agilidade à resposta.

A outra frente é a entrada do Brasil na rede mundial de sangue raro , prevista para este mês. Com a adesão, o Brasil poderá pedir ajuda a outros países e também ser acionado por eles.

A mudança vale sobretudo para pacientes com um tipo de sangue comum em outra região do mundo, mas muito raro aqui, para os quais não existe doador no país e a bolsa teria de vir de fora.

articles.title: Chris Hemsworth and Elsa Pataky helped return Tasmanian devils to mainland Australia after 3,000 years; the endangered marsupials could help restore ecosystems
articles.summary: For the first time in 3,000 years, the Tasmanian devil is back in the wild on mainland Australia.
articles.body: For the first time in 3,000 years, the Tasmanian devil is back in the wild on mainland Australia. The actors Chris Hemsworth and Elsa Pataky helped release some of the animals, including Lenny and Lisa, into a 400-hectare wildlife sanctuary on Barrington Tops in New South Wales. Aussie Ark carried out the release with Global Wildlife Conservation and WildArk. Eleven devils were released into the sanctuary, and 20 more were planned for 2020. Twenty-six devils now live in the wild on the Australian mainland, after a trial release of 15 devils preceded the main release on 10 September.How did Chris Hemsworth help release Tasmanian devilsAussie Ark, working with Global Wildlife Conservation and WildArk, released 11 Tasmanian devils into a 400-hectare (nearly 1,000 acres) wildlife sanctuary on Barrington Tops. WildArk states that Hemsworth and Pataky helped release some of the animals, including Lenny and Lisa, into their new home.According to the World Economic Forum, the actor couple joined conservation groups last month to release the 11 animals into a wildlife sanctuary in New South Wales. It describes Hemsworth as best known for playing Thor in Marvel Cinematic Universe films, and says he spoke of laying traps to catch the devils before releasing them into the wild. Tim Faulkner, president of Aussie Ark, said: "This release of devils will be the first of many."Why did Tasmanian devils disappear from mainland AustraliaAccording to WildArk, Tasmanian devils vanished from mainland Australia in large part because of introduced dingoes, which hunt in packs. Dingoes never reached Tasmania. The devils were wiped out on the mainland after being hunted by dingoes, a pack animal, and were left confined to the island state.In Tasmania, a transmissible, painful and fatal disease called Devil Facial Tumour Disease, the only known contagious cancer, decimated up to 90 per cent of the wild population, leaving just 25,000 devils in the wild there. The World Economic Forum says numbers in Tasmania have dropped since the 1990s because of facial tumour disease. It adds that the devil, the world's largest surviving marsupial carnivore, is about the size of a small dog and was listed as endangered on the Red List in 2008.How will the sanctuary protect Tasmanian devilsThe 400-hectare sanctuary on Barrington Tops will prevent the spread of disease, feral pests, noxious weeds and fire. It described fire as catastrophic for the country earlier in the year. The sanctuary will also keep cars out, so that the devils learn not to associate cars with food. WildArk says that association could be deadly when the animals are more widely released.Aussie Ark chose the devils for release because they were the most suitable to breed with one another without inbreeding. For the past decade, the Aussie Ark team has been building an insurance population and studying the animals' reproductive physiology, behaviour and ecological needs. The release took place on 10 September and followed a successful assisted trial release of 15 devils. WildArk states that 26 devils now live in the wild on the mainland.How will Tasmanian devils help restore Australian ecosystemsFaulkner said that in 100 years people will look back on the day as the one that set in motion "the ecological restoration of an entire country". He said the devil will engineer the environment around it, restoring and rebalancing forest ecology after centuries of devastation from introduced foxes, cats and other invasive predators.Aussie Ark has been breeding young devils and plans to release 20 more next year and another 20 the year after. It reports that Aussie Ark has bred nearly 400 joeys and can now return some of them to the wild. Mark Hutchinson, co-founder of WildArk, said the reintroduction is paving the way for future introductions that are already being mapped out. articles.title: Rock legend Rick Wakeman played piano for 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam; he now wants the last 125 bears still caged on bile farms moved to sanctuaries
articles.summary: Most pianists perform for crowds that clap, cheer, and request encores.
articles.body: Most pianists perform for crowds that clap, cheer, and request encores. Rick Wakeman, the celebrated keyboard player from the band Yes, on the other hand, recently played live for a very different audience, more than 150 rescued moon bears in a Vietnamese forest sanctuary. The concert was joyful, but it emerged not only out of his love for the wildlife but also carried an urgent purpose. Wakeman wants the last 125 bears still locked in cages on old bile farms moved to sanctuaries before more of them die. Here’s what happened at the concert, how the bears reacted, and why moon bears need protection.How Rick Wakeman played a grand piano for more than 150 rescued moon bears in a Vietnamese sanctuaryThe Guardian reported on Thursday, 24 September 2026, that Wakeman, a former member of Yes who went on to a prolific solo career, performed live on a Yamaha grand piano in Animals Asia's bear sanctuary in Tam Dao National Park, Vietnam. He had written new compositions especially for the rescued bears. The charity Animals Asia runs the sanctuary. Wakeman, who supports animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, held the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions so their bile can be extracted. He also joked about the weather, telling the newspaper the heat was double that of the English heatwave, and that a fan would only blow more hot air around.The new pieces Wakeman wrote for Moon Bears Dawn and MoonRolling Stone, in a report, described the show as a private concert in which Wakeman sat at a grand piano and played new music written for the bears. He performed two new pieces about the rescued moon bears Dawn and Moon, along with two songs about bears called Cyril Wolverine and Rocky (The Legacy). Video of the performance shows several bears coming to the edge of the enclosure to listen. Wakeman has sponsored rescued bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one, a big 20-month-old male. When Wakeman visited, the young bear came to the edge of the enclosure, stood on his back legs, and stared at him, which Wakeman called brilliant.Why Wakeman refused to play The Teddy Bear's Picnic for his audienceWakeman joked before the performance that he would not be playing the well-known children's song about a teddy bear's picnic. Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said they had little choice, but that all animals react to music, especially gentle, melodic music, so he planned to play exactly that and hoped the bears would come to the edge of the sanctuary to listen. His experience at home shapes that belief. He plays music for his rescue dogs and cats in Suffolk, and said that his dogs walk out if they dislike a piece, while his cats do not enjoy metal, grunge, or rap and want a melody. One cat used to jump on his grand piano and rattle the strings until he started playing again.Why Moon Bears are rescued from Vietnam's bile farms and how the illegal trade harms Asiatic black bearsAccording to a 2015 report from Phys.org, Bile is taken from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by inserting a needle into the gallbladder and drawing the fluid out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in several countries, including China and Vietnam. Vietnam has just banned the practice, yet some bears remain in cramped enclosures. The trade is the fourth biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in East Asia and has caused a dramatic decline in Asiatic black bear numbers in Vietnam. Nearly a third of their numbers around the world have been lost in just 30 years. Wakeman said that before rescue, many bears were chained in cages for 10 or 20 years, in conditions where they could not even turn around.Why Wakeman wants the last 125 caged bears moved to sanctuariesThe concert's message is urgent. Wakeman said he is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and to urge the government to release them. According to Wakeman, the sanctuary holds 150 bears, but 125 remain in cages in the old bear bile farms, and four die each month. He said they must be moved to the sanctuary quickly. Wakeman said it is moving to watch the rescued bears, which he described as not tame but very safe and very happy, and he saw two of them playing in a bubble bath. He added that some of them had never set their feet on grass before. Doctor Jill Robinson, the founder and chief executive officer of Animals Asia, said the charity is beyond blessed to have his support and that his love for the bears can be heard in the haunting music he wrote for them.How readers can support bear rescue and keep attention on the 125 bears still waiting in old bile farmsThe Press Association via Irish News reported that Animals Asia has a petition urging the prime minister of Vietnam to help the charity free the bears still stuck in bile farms. It can be signed on the charity's website. Signing, sharing the story, and supporting rescue organisations are practical ways to keep attention on the bears while time is short. If Wakeman's numbers are right, every month of delay costs more animals their chance at a life in a sanctuary.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Air India, Akasa Air and IndiGo have temporarily suspended or curtailed flights to Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, following reports of explosions, including a loud blast at the city’s international airport, on Thursday.Akasa Air suspended flights to and from Riyadh through Saturday, while IndiGo cancelled its Riyadh services through Friday.Air India said a flight from Delhi to Riyadh returned to Delhi on Thursday and was subsequently cancelled “in the interest of safety”. The airline also suspended all flights to and from Riyadh until Saturday.Lufthansa Group, the German aviation company that owns Lufthansa Airlines and other European carriers, said its airlines would suspend flights to Riyadh through October 16 “due to current developments in the Middle East.”Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has claimed responsibility for the latest attack on Riyadh’s airport, saying a ballistic missile had caused damage, but provided no evidence. The group’s military spokesperson later said the Houthis had fired additional ballistic and cruise missiles at airports in Riyadh and the southwestern city of Najran, claiming the strikes had disrupted flights.Riyadh’s airport had “closed again”, global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said on X on Thursday afternoon. It reported that the last landing had taken place more than 80 minutes earlier and the last takeoff more than 90 minutes earlier.The developments came amid heightened safety concerns following a series of Houthi attacks on Saudi airports on October 6 and 7. Saudi authorities, as cited by the BBC, said a separate attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh had killed one person and injured eight others. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had targeted Saudi airports using ballistic missiles and drones.India on Thursday condemned the attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, calling the targeting of civilian infrastructure “completely unacceptable”.“India condemns the attacks over the past few days targeting Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which have resulted in civilian deaths and injuries,” the Ministry of External Affairs said.“We express our deepest condolences to the families of those who have lost their loved ones. articles.title: Christa Pike's health has seen 'profound turnaround' in last three days, lawyers say
articles.summary: Pike's lawyers say her recovery is "remarkable" as they give an update on her condition after she survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
articles.body:
Christa Pike has made a "profound" turnaround after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, her lawyers say.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

In a statement on Thursday, Pike's lawyers described her recovery as "remarkable" and said she is able to walk with assistance and is eating. She has also regained some movement in her arms, which were badly injured during the attempted execution, they said.

"Physicians are encouraged by her physical recovery," the statement said.

The case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

"Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die," her legal team said.

Pike's lawyers said they do not know the full emotional and psychological toll of the execution attempt or how long it will take her to recover.

They added that while she struggles to process what happened, she "continues to express concern for others, particularly the family of her victim Colleen Slemmer".

Slemmer's mother, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death, has branded the failed execution a "mess".

Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.

Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.

Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method?

A court has ordered officials to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution, which could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.

On Wednesday, Judge I'Ashea Myles ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, such as packaging, inserts and labels.

The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition before, during and after the failed execution.

She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions for the rest of the year and said he wants answers about what went wrong.

Pike's lawyers have called on the governor to downgrade Pike's punishment to life in prison without parole.

Proponents of capital punishment have suggested using a different method to put her to death.

articles.title: In 2011, an Ohio man was served foreclosure papers on his $4.5 million, 17,000-sq-ft mansion; after nearly 15 years of hearings, mediation and court fights, an eviction notice has now been approved
articles.summary: According to reporting by Realtor.com and News 5 Cleveland, along with Ohio court records, an unusually long foreclosure battle involving a sprawling
articles.body: According to reporting by Realtor.com and News 5 Cleveland, along with Ohio court records, an unusually long foreclosure battle involving a sprawling mansion in Aurora, Ohio, has reached another turning point. A magistrate has approved the eviction of Louis Telerico, who has continued living at the property despite the home changing ownership. The 17,000-square-foot estate, located at 545 Bristol Drive in the Barrington Estates community near a golf course, became the subject of a foreclosure case filed by Bank of America in August 2011. Court records show that the case remained active for years as Telerico pursued appeals and bankruptcy proceedings.The foreclosure was eventually finalized after the Ohio Court of Appeals upheld the sale in December 2025. According to the appellate court, the property had been sold to Bank of America through a sheriff’s sale in January 2025, with the trial court confirming the sale several months later. The bank subsequently transferred the property, which was later sold to investment company ERADAL in July 2026 for slightly more than $3 million.Yet the change in ownership did not immediately end Telerico’s time at the mansion. After acquiring the property, ERADAL began the process of removing him from the home. The company served a three-day notice to vacate in July and filed an eviction complaint after he remained at the residence. The investment firm also raised concerns about the condition of the property, including deterioration around the roof and heavily overgrown grounds.Local reporting by News 5 Cleveland found that ERADAL had already begun work on the estate while the legal proceedings continued. The company treated portions of the grounds, marked trees for removal and assessed damage to the house as it prepared for future improvements.The extraordinary length of the foreclosure appears to have been driven by a combination of legal appeals, bankruptcy filings and delays within the court system. Ohio appellate records confirm that the original foreclosure complaint dates back to 2011, while the final appeal concerning the sale was still being litigated in 2025. The appeals court ultimately affirmed the lower court’s decision. The latest eviction ruling, however, may not be the final chapter.Telerico’s attorney has indicated that negotiations are underway that could allow his former home to be purchased back. The proposed deal would depend on Telerico securing financing, leaving open the possibility that he could regain ownership rather than be removed from the property.ERADAL has indicated that it is willing to allow time for a potential transaction, but the company is also preparing to take control of the estate and begin restoring it if a purchase agreement does not materialise. For now, the legal battle that began during the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis has moved into a very different phase. Telerico is no longer fighting simply to prevent a foreclosure sale. He is now attempting to secure financing to buy back a property that has already passed through foreclosure and changed hands.The case stands out not only because of the value and size of the mansion, but because of how long the homeowner remained in the property after the foreclosure proceedings began. Nearly 15 years after the original case was filed, the question is no longer whether the property will change hands, but whether Telerico can find a way to remain its owner.You use AI every day. articles.title: Russian strikes and approaching winter force some in Kyiv to pack bags and flee
articles.summary: A renewed Russian campaign of strikes on power and energy infrastructure has made some contemplate leaving Ukraine's capital.
articles.body:
As Russia's attacks on Ukraine's cities intensify and autumn's cooler temperatures hint at another tough winter to come, Ukrainians are wrestling with how to meet the twin challenges ahead: Russian drone and missile strikes and the biting cold.

"It was a very difficult winter last year in Kyiv," says mother of two Mariia Shostak, who is now packing her bags and leaving her small flat.

With prolonged periods of sub-zero temperatures and frequent power cuts brought about by Russia's attack on the country's power grid, last winter was one of the hardest so far.

"There were some days and weeks that were unbearable. I started thinking I'm not going through another winter like this."

Mariia is not even waiting for winter. Russia's latest assaults on the capital have forced her hand.

"Everything changed in late August and the beginning of September, when Kyiv started being attacked around the clock," she said.

"Earlier, the drones and missiles were intercepted somewhere on the outskirts. Now it was happening in the centre, right above our heads."

After weeks of escalating Russian attacks, which by the end of September had included petrol stations, power plants and key bridges over the Dnipro river, Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko said the city was facing a "very dramatic situation".

Mariia's children, four-year-old Artur and Kira, who's two, were both born after Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

Unwilling to subject them to another miserable, dangerous winter, she's taking them abroad. They plan to spend the winter in Hurghada, on Egypt's Red Sea coast. It's cheaper than Europe, Mariia explains, and warmer too.

"I don't feel safe in Ukraine in any way," she says.

Polls show that many Ukrainians are feeling the same way, even if not everyone has yet made such a radical decision.

A September survey by the Gradus research company found that 40% of Ukrainians were considering relocating if living conditions continued to deteriorate; 35% said they would not move elsewhere, while 25% were undecided.

"People are thinking about a combination of stress factors," Evgeniya Blyznyuk, Gradus's founder and CEO, told us. "Not just about electricity and blackouts like last winter. Russians are targeting big logistics centres, which means that the population is worrying about products, about food during the winter."

Russia's recent attacks on Kyiv's bridges, petrol stations and schools have increased the sense of danger and foreboding.

For families with young children, the situation feels especially urgent.

Last winter, Iryna, who asked us not to use her surname, says her three-year-old daughter Polina found it hard to cope.

"Sometimes we didn't have heating for weeks and the temperature inside the apartment was zero or five degrees," she tells us. "So being here with a little child that is sick all the time was not OK."

The family's recent experiences have only compounded Polina's difficulties.

"We had two missile attacks this year," Iryna says.

The first explosion, in early June, blew out several windows in the family's home on the north-western edge of Kyiv. A month later, after some of the damage had been repaired, a second blast, close to the foot of their 10-storey apartment block, propelled a wave of earth into the flat, forcing the family to move into temporary accommodation.

Polina's health has deteriorated. She suffers from extreme anxiety, which has brought on bouts of incontinence, vomiting and uncontrollable shaking.

"Now we have this neurological problem with her so that's the reason we're thinking about leaving," Iryna says. "There are new symptoms after each shelling."

Iryna, whose husband is in the army, has not yet decided where to go. Her work with an international NGO may allow her to work remotely from Poland.

"Our president says that it is better to leave Kyiv because this is target number one," she says.

For other Kyiv residents, the solution lies closer to home: in the vast open spaces of Ukraine's countryside.

Olena Konoplia tells us she spent weeks looking for a suitable location before settling on a cottage in a rural community two hours outside the capital.

"I decided the better option will be a little village without any factories, any [warehouses] and any railway stations," Olena explains.

"Everything that can be a Russian target."

On the day we visited, Olena was busy ferrying supplies to the house and supervising the installation of a new door.

In keeping with Ukrainian tradition, a priest has already been around to bless her new home.

The cottage has gas-powered convection heaters, but in an adjacent barn a stack of firewood will help to keep Olena warm in the event of power cuts. She has already installed high-speed internet, necessary for her work at a Kyiv-based charitable foundation.

At a time when air raid sirens sound constantly in Kyiv and explosions can be heard almost every day, the peace and quiet of the village is what Olena says she needs most.

"After several nights here, when I can sleep, just sleep, without any explosions, without any sirens, I feel better," she says. "I can work, write my articles, I feel good."

Olena's elderly mother will soon be joining her.

"She lives in a pretty dangerous district in Kyiv and it's harmful for her health," she explains.

Of course, not everyone can afford a cottage in the countryside or a months-long trip abroad.

Most Kyiv residents will do what they can to survive another tough winter in the capital, just as they have before.

The authorities are taking steps to prepare. Some of Kyiv's most vulnerable citizens – the elderly and women with young children – are being offered places in converted sanatoriums and rehabilitation centres in the city's forested outskirts.

Meanwhile, a network of around 15 small-scale power plants has been constructed around the city over the past 18 months in an effort to shore up Kyiv's battered power grid.

The plants, constructed in fortified bunkers and protected from drone attack by huge steel cages, are each capable of providing electricity and heat to several hundred of the city's high-rise apartment blocks.

But with energy companies already talking about scheduled power cuts and supermarkets experiencing periodic shortages of some goods, the pressures to leave are growing.

Evgeniya Blyznyuk says she does not expect to see a mass exodus from the capital and says most people have yet to make up their minds, reluctant to jeopardise their jobs or take children out of school.

"They will postpone it until conditions become really unliveable," she says.

Additional reporting by Mariana Matveichuk and Anastasiia Levchenko.

articles.title: UK robotics hubs to drive adoption of new tech
articles.summary: The government says the hubs will support businesses and public services across the country.
articles.body:
Eight new Robotics Adoption Hubs are to be rolled out across the UK, the government has announced.

The hubs will get £40m to offer advice and support to businesses and public services looking to use the latest technologies and switch to automation.

One, in Newcastle, will help healthcare providers adopt robotic-assisted surgery while another, in Lincoln, will assist the farming and food industries with innovations such as automated fruit-picking machines.

AI and Robotics Minister Kanishka Narayan said harnessing robotics "in every sector of our economy" could "speed up how we reindustrialise the UK".

On a visit to Lincoln Institute for Agri-Food Technology to announce a new £6.3m HARVEST hub, Narayan said he was "confident" British innovation "can stand the test internationally if we keep up the future of technology".

He was shown automated robots moving along strawberry crops, another moving across a ploughed field and a third shooting pulses of concentrated light on to soil to boil and kill the cells of a weed.

"Farmers are really struggling to be able to find workers to pick fruit when they need them and in some cases that means a big change in the cost, and so clearly that element of farming has changed and the question is how we can support our farmers to stay in business," he said.

"I've witnessed first hand, even in combine harvesters and robotics in dairy farming, how much of a change that's made in British farming by this technology and I'm hoping today's announcement will make a big contribution to that."

Professor Simon Pearson MBE of the Lincoln Institute for Agri-Food Technology, part of the University of Lincoln, said the hub would introduce the new technologies to the farming and food sectors.

"Industry needs robots to drive productivity, whether it's on farms or food factory, so the hub will bring the food and robot companies together," he said.

"Farming is changing at a phenomenal rate and it's very difficult with profitability, labour access and climate issues and these technologies won't resolve those issues but they will help.

"We have world-class food and farming companies in the hub, including Dyson Farming, and to be world-class you've got to be internationally competitive and if we don't do it in Lincolnshire other countries will do it."

The eight new Robotics Adoption Hubs are:

The Newcastle Surgical Hub, which will get £7.4m in investment.

The Greater Southwest Robotics Adoption Hub, supporting robotic adoption in industries such as maritime, energy and food packaging.

RoboPass Plus, based in Milton Keynes to support the rollout of service robots, drones and driverless cars.

Hwb Llwybr Roboteg Cymru, supporting manufacturing firms

National Waste and Recycling Robotics Adoption Hub, based in the South East.

The Yorkshire Robotics Adoption Hub, working with universities in Bradford and Huddersfield to support manufacturers with automation.

South Wales Robotics Adoption Hub, based in Swansea and supporting small businesses to adopt robotics and automation.

As well as the eight hubs, the programme will provide £2.5m to support 12 projects to develop practical robotics training and apprenticeships, including the Port and Logistics Robotics Adoption Programme in Hull.

articles.title: Why did country singer Dolly Parton recorded Jolene in Welsh?
articles.summary: The cover of smash-hit Jolene, with Welsh and English lyrics, is released on Friday.
articles.body:
A Welsh language collaboration between Dolly Parton, her niece Jada Star and singer-songwriter Bronwen Lewis might not have been on your bingo card for this year.

But their cover of smash-hit Jolene, with Welsh and English lyrics, has been released on Friday.

The song, recorded before Parton's death on 25 August , is her second posthumous single.

A teaser video released last week shows how Parton spent some time understanding the phonetics of Lewis' translation and recorded her parts at her studio in Nashville in early 2025.

Lewis, a proud Welsh speaker from Neath, started translating some of her favourite tunes in 2024, landed on the Parton classic and recorded a video of herself singing it.

"I never expected it would go viral and definitely didn't expect it to attract the attention of Dolly's family - especially her niece Jada," Lewis said.

Star, also a singer-songwriter, came over to Wales from Nashville and bonded instantly with BBC Radio Wales' Lewis.

The teaser revealed it was Star's suggestion to record Jolene in Welsh, and she would get her aunt involved too.

Star and Lewis said Parton, who has links to Machynlleth in Powys , was "proud" to sing in Welsh.

On the track, Parton recites that "heartbreak sounds the same in every language".

Five facts about Dolly Parton's Welsh heritage

In 2008, during a concert at the Cardiff International Arena, Parton reportedly revealed her Welsh ancestry to fans in the crowd.

She said she had visited Wales "about three times" and it "felt good because it feels like family", when speaking to WalesOnline.

Star revealed one side of the family from Parton's mother Avie Lee Owens was initially believed to have come from Conwy.

Some of Parton's music may have been inspired by her Welsh roots, according to Star.

Following the singer's death, research by staff at Conwy council's archives suggested Parton's ancestors were from Machynlleth, in Powys, not Conwy as previously thought.

Fans across the world reacted to the news of the new single.

"Really looking forward to hearing this version," one commented

"Cannot wait for this," another said while another fan commented "anghygoel", which translates to amazing.

This is not the first time Parton has featured on songs in another language.

She has appeared on several Latin songs and also collaborated on a track with an Irish folk band in 2011.

Before her death, Parton revealed she had recorded a song with U2 which is set to be released in November. She also teased fans about a track which has been kept in a time capsule until its planned release in 2046.

articles.title: Alderney flights cancelled due to 'unprecedented' crew sickness
articles.summary: Upcoming Skybus flights between Guernsey and Alderney and Alderney and Southampton are affected.
articles.body:
An airline has warned it is unable to operate several of its upcoming flights due to "an unprecedented level of crew sickness".

Guernsey States-owned airline Aurigny said on Thursday that it had been advised of the issue by Skybus, the airline it contracts to operate services to and from Alderney .

Skybus CEO Stuart Reid apologised "unreservedly" for the impact on services between Guernsey and Alderney and Alderney and Southampton until 16 October.

Aurigny said rumours that all of its services to and from Alderney were being cancelled in the next few days were incorrect and said the "majority of the airline's planned schedule is expected to operate".

The airline also said it was "working to minimise the impact on passengers wherever possible".

"Unfortunately, the late notice provided by Skybus has impacted our ability to respond as promptly as customers rightly expect," a statement from Aurigny said.

It said passengers were being contacted directly by the airline or their travel agent and alternative transport would be arranged where possible.

Reid added: "We recognise that the level of service provided by Skybus at present neither meets Aurigny's expectations nor the needs of the community.

"We remain committed to working closely with our colleagues at Aurigny to improve the reliability of the service we provide."

articles.title: America First, powered by foreign talent; five of six tech execs honored by Trump were born outside US
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: There was something deliciously awkward and ironic about US President Donald Trump’s celebration of American
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: There was something deliciously awkward and ironic about US President Donald Trump’s celebration of American technological greatness in the White House on Thursday. Of the six technology titans who received the nation’s highest science and tech honours from the MAGA boss, five were born outside the United States. The sole exception was Michael Dell, the Texas-born founder of Dell Technologies.If the MAGA movement’s proposition is that America does not need foreigners to make America great, the White House assembled a plush rebuttal -- complete with medals, billionaires, and a presidential seal of approval. At the ceremony, titled “Science: A New Golden Age,” Trump presented the National Medal of Science to Tesla’s Elon Musk, Google co-founder Sergey Brin, Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Dell received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.The honours recognised extraordinary contributions to computing, semiconductors, artificial intelligence and space exploration. They also offered an inadvertent reminder of a longstanding truth about Silicon Valley and the wider American tech industry: US sci- tech primacy has been built not merely on American ingenuity, but on its ability to attract, educate and retain talent from around the world. That is a slightly inconvenient message for an administration determined to make foreign workers villains in its political narrative.Nobody had a more surreal day on this front than Satya Nadella. In the morning, vice-president JD Vance was unloading on Microsoft, accusing it of abusing employment-based immigration programs while laying off American workers. Vance cited 6,000 US job cuts alongside 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards, announcing that the administration was suspending the company from the program used to sponsor permanent residency for eligible foreign workers. Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented a wholesale replacement of American employees, saying most were for existing workers.Hours later, there was Nadella in the White House, receiving a presidential medal for helping build one of America’s most consequential technology companies -- from a shambolic administration that managed, in a single working day, to put Microsoft in the immigration penalty box and its chief executive on the national innovation podium. The citation for Nadella praised his “transformative leadership of a critical American technology company, which led to its rejuvenation for a new era of cloud computing,” and his role in building “the hyperscale infrastructure that enabled the training and global deployment of American super intelligence.”It was a substantial tribute to the Hyderabad-born executive’s transformation of Microsoft into a cloud-computing and artificial-intelligence powerhouse. It was also a reminder that the company’s leadership, like much of the talent sustaining Silicon Valley, does not conform neatly to an America-first immigration script.Vance’s argument is that foreign workers can displace Americans and become vulnerable to employers because their immigration status is tied to their jobs. While tech executives acknowledge that concern deserves scrutiny where companies exploit visa programmes, a blanket hostility to foreign talent is a rather different proposition -- particularly when the administration simultaneously celebrates executives whose achievements have helped make American companies global leaders. “A foreign worker is a problem when applying for a green card but a national treasure when collecting a medal,” one industry insider remarked tartly after the event, asserting that foreign-born tech leaders don’t arrive in the US as geniuses; America is what makes them.Jensen Huang and Lisa Su supplied another irony, this time with a geopolitical edge. Cousins once removed, both were born in Taiwan. Huang has built Nvidia into the dominant force in AI computing, while Su has led AMD’s revival as a formidable competitor in high-performance processors. Their achievements illustrate how Taiwan-born engineering talent has helped shape the technologies on which America’s economic and strategic ambitions increasingly depend.Their recognition comes against the backdrop of Trump’s outreach to Beijing, including his recent high-profile engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Some foreign-policy analysts worry that a transactional approach to relations with China, or concessions made in pursuit of a broader accommodation, could weaken the credibility of America’s commitment to Taiwan’s security. While the medal ceremony did not itself signal any change in US policy towards Taiwan, the juxtaposition was striking: Washington was celebrating two Taiwanese-born executives whose work is central to the global semiconductor industry even as the future of Taiwan remains one of the most consequential questions in US-China relations. Like Nadella, Huang and Su are living illustrations of how global talent reinforce American power. None of that fits comfortably into the MAGA proposition that national greatness can be secured by shutting the door on immigrants.Meanwhile, Sergei Brin and Elon Musk offered another reminder of the complicated origins of American tech success. Brin, born in Moscow in the erstwhile Soviet Union, emigrated to the U.S when he was a child, and went on to co-found Google, helping transform how the world searches for and organises information. Musk, meanwhile, was born in South Africa before moving to America and eventually becoming a US citizen. Through Tesla and SpaceX, he has helped reshape electric vehicles, commercial spaceflight and satellite communications. His relationship with Trump has had its own spectacular ruptures and reconciliations, making his presence at the ceremony -- on a day he has been lashing out at India and its business leadership -- another reminder that the administration’s relationship with tech leaders is rarely short of drama.You use AI every day. They were taken out with the help of a crane. articles.title: Lucknow Metro extends free GoSmart card exchange till Oct 16
articles.summary: LUCKNOW: Lucknow Metro has extended the deadline for commuters to exchange existing GoSmart cards for National Common Mobility Cards (NCMC) free of cost
articles.body: LUCKNOW: Lucknow Metro has extended the deadline for commuters to exchange existing GoSmart cards for National Common Mobility Cards (NCMC) free of cost until Oct 16. The facility, which was due to end on Oct 9, is available at all metro stations.More than 55,000 passengers have exchanged their GoSmart cards for NCMC cards so far, the Uttar Pradesh Metro Rail Corporation (UPMRC) said in a press release on Friday.Existing cardholders must use up their remaining GoSmart balance before visiting a station. They can then surrender the card and collect an NCMC free of charge during the extended period.UPMRC managing director Sushil Kumar said the extension would give remaining cardholders more time to make the switch. He urged passengers to use the facility and move to the unified mobility card.The NCMC, also known as “One Nation One Card”, can be used on Lucknow Metro and, subject to interoperability arrangements, on participating metro systems, buses, parking facilities and retail outlets. The card also offers a 10% discount on every journey on Lucknow Metro.New users can buy an NCMC at metro stations for a non-refundable issuance charge of Rs 100. Cards can be recharged through station kiosks, ticket vending machines, the Airtel app and other compatible channels. Records show Peters, a native of Canada, paid $6.45 million for the property in 2017. The estate is anchored by an 11,600-square-foot mansion built in 1998, with eight bedrooms and nine bathrooms. Outside, a resort-style space includes a swimming pool, spa, waterfall, gazebo, playground and putting green. Hidden Hills is a gated city centred around large lots and equestrian activities.What did Russell Peters’ 1.5-acre Hidden Hills estate featureAccording to The Los Angeles Times, Hidden Hills is a gated city centred around large lots and equestrian activities. articles.body: NEW DELHI: The government has advised major social media platforms to "identify unlawful content and prioritise action based on complaints" from authorised including law enforcement agencies, PTI reported quoting sources.The ministry of electronics and information technology (MeitY) is learnt to have issued an advisory to social media companies on October 8, expressing concern over the online circulation of information related to the protests that is allegedly false, misleading, manipulated or presented out of context.“MeitY has advised large social media platforms to identify such unlawful content and prioritise action based on complaints received from authorised government bodies,” an official source aware of the development told PTI.The ministry warned that such content could disturb public order and social tranquillity, raise law and order concerns and incite violence.The advisory has also asked social media platforms to label synthetically generated content, particularly when it is presented as depicting ongoing events.The ministry has stressed the need for timely cooperation between social media companies and law enforcement agencies to address unlawful content and provide information when required.“MeitY has advised social media companies to ensure timely cooperation with law enforcement and other authorised government agencies for action and furnishing information as well as provide assistance as per the applicable law within stipulated timelines under the IT Rules, 2021,” the source added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Protest without permission not in accordance with law': SC on CJP's October 10 Jantar Mantar stir
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A team of senior advocates led by Kapil Sibal moved the Supreme Court on Friday, challenging the cancellation of trains and proposed closure of
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A team of senior advocates led by Kapil Sibal moved the Supreme Court on Friday, challenging the cancellation of trains and proposed closure of Metro stations in Delhi ahead of the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) October 10 protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant questioned why the protesters had not challenged the Delhi Police's decision to deny permission for the demonstration at Jantar Mantar.The court observed that unless the denial of permission was challenged, it could not consider relaxing the restrictions imposed ahead of the protest."If there is no permission for protests, it will be an unlawful protest," Justice Joymalya Bagchi observed.Sibal, appearing for CPM MP M A Baby, argued that every citizen had the right to protest, even spontaneously.The Supreme Court said the right to peaceful protest at a designated place existed, but holding a demonstration without permission could expose protesters to prosecution.The bench also indicated that it could consider easing the restrictions if the organisers challenged the denial of permission and provided assurances about the proposed gathering. The court said it could seek details about the number of people expected to attend and undertakings that protesters would remain peaceful and not carry weapons.Based on these assurances, the court said it could consider relaxing restrictions imposed to prevent a possible law and order situation.Meanwhile, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke questioned the Delhi Police's decision to deny permission for the October 10 protest, arguing that Jantar Mantar was a designated protest site and that police permission was not required to hold a demonstration there.Dipke also criticised the Centre over the cancellation of trains to Delhi ahead of Saturday's protest."Shut down entire country if you are scared of youth," he said, taking aim at the government over the restrictions.Delhi Police had earlier denied permission for the CJP's proposed protest at Jantar Mantar on October 10, citing short notice, alleged violations during a previous demonstration and concerns over public safety, law and order and traffic management.Joint commissioner of police Nupur Prasad said the police had received an application from CJP co-convener Saurav Das seeking permission for a protest over the accountability of the Chief Election Commissioner."This intimation was considered, and it was found that the intimation was given in a very short span of time, whereas as per the prescribed guideline, the intimation has to be received 10 days prior to the protest that is planned," she said.Prasad also pointed to the party's conduct during an earlier protest at the same venue."Further, it is also important to mention that on an earlier occasion, when the Cockroach Janta Party was given permission to hold a protest there, they did not follow the lawful directions and did not follow their own undertakings given at that point in time," she said.She added that Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which allows preventive restrictions to maintain public order, was in force in the New Delhi area. The police warned that anyone violating the restrictions could face legal action.The restrictions come ahead of the CJP's planned protest on Saturday, with several trains to New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin cancelled and restrictions proposed at metro stations.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Isabella Rossellini turned a 27-acre New York farmstead into a protected community farm after conserving 20.8 acres; Mama Farm now runs a member CSA and biodiversity programmes for families and children
articles.summary: A wooded property on Long Island has become a place where farming, animal care and community activities share the same space.
articles.body: A wooded property on Long Island has become a place where farming, animal care and community activities share the same space. The project is Mama Farm, founded by actress Isabella Rossellini in Brookhaven, New York, in 2013. According to the Peconic Land Trust, Rossellini donated a conservation easement in 2012 that protects 20.8 acres of the property. The farm combines food production with biodiversity initiatives and educational activities for families and children. Its community-supported agriculture programme also connects members with the food grown on the land, making the property a working example of how conservation and community life can go hand in hand.From a wooded property to a protected farmsteadRossellini established Mama Farm with the idea of bringing agriculture and nature together. The original 27-acre property provided space for growing food while retaining its woodland character. Protecting the land became an important part of the project. The Peconic Land Trust helped conserve 20.8 acres through a conservation easement. This legal arrangement restricts certain forms of development and land use to preserve a property's natural or agricultural value. The land remains privately owned, but the agreement helps protect it from development that could compromise its conservation purpose.The arrangement is particularly relevant on Long Island, where development can put pressure on open spaces and agricultural land. Protecting most of the property helps ensure that farming and nature remain part of its future. Mama Farm's current website describes the property as 28 acres, while earlier accounts refer to the original farmstead as 27 acres. Its activities have also expanded beyond growing food to include animal care, biodiversity and environmental education.Growing food while caring for biodiversityAt Mama Farm, farming practices are closely connected with its environmental goals. According to the farm's official website, crops are grown from heirloom seeds using organic and regenerative agricultural techniques. Farmer Patty Gentry is associated with its growing operations. The farm says it avoids pesticides, herbicides, insecticides and environmentally harmful fertilisers. These practices reflect its aim of producing food while limiting the potential impact of agriculture on the surrounding environment.Animals are another part of the property. Its sanctuary includes heritage-breed chickens and turkeys, sheep, goats, quail, ducks and other animals. According to Mama Farm, the animals are not slaughtered, although eggs and honey are among the products offered through its community-supported agriculture programme. The use of heirloom seeds and heritage breeds also highlights the importance of agricultural diversity. By keeping traditional varieties and breeds part of a working farm, Mama Farm connects food production with the preservation of older agricultural practices.How the community-supported agriculture programme worksMama Farm runs a community-supported agriculture (CSA) programme through which members receive shares of the farm's produce. The model creates a direct connection between the people growing food and those who consume it. Mama Farm offers eggs and honey through its CSA programme, while vegetable shares are arranged with farmer Patty Gentry. The programme connects members with local food production and gives them a closer understanding of where their food comes from.The programme also helps make farming more accessible. Growing food requires planning, attention to the seasons and ongoing care for the land. A CSA gives members a closer view of that process and encourages a relationship with the farm that goes beyond shopping. At Mama Farm, the programme forms part of a wider effort to bring people closer to agriculture while maintaining the property's role as a protected working landscape.Children's activities, workshops and a place to gatherMama Farm's work extends beyond food production. Its activities include workshops, children's programmes, theatre and avant-garde films, offering visitors different ways to explore environmental themes and community life. The farm's website describes its atmosphere as inspired by the Italian piazza, a traditional public square where people gather and exchange ideas. This concept reflects the intention to create a shared space where visitors can spend time together, learn and engage with their surroundings.Children can encounter farm animals and explore the outdoors, while workshops provide opportunities to learn about nature and agriculture. These activities bring environmental themes into the farm's community programmes. The conservation easement provides a foundation for these initiatives by helping protect the land on which they take place.Mama Farm brings together sustainable agriculture, animal care and community participation, showing how protected land can remain productive and accessible. Through the project, Rossellini has linked the preservation of a New York farmstead with practical activities that connect people to food, animals and the natural environment. Its approach demonstrates how conservation can become part of everyday community life while helping safeguard agricultural land for the future.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient.
